title: Rounding rules and estimation
blurb: Round to any place correctly, decide when real life says round up or down, and estimate fast to check answers.
question: A 10 mL vial holds a drug given in 0.75 mL doses, and a clinic needs syringes for 250 patients in boxes of 24. How many full doses are in the vial, and how many boxes must be ordered?

teach.body: Formally, rounding replaces a number with the nearest value at a chosen place (tenths, hundreds, whole numbers), and estimating uses rounded or compatible numbers to get an approximate answer quickly. In plain English: rounding tidies a number to the precision you need; estimating lets you sanity-check a calculator answer in seconds. On the TEAS, the stem tells you the place, and the context tells you whether to go up or down.

items: Underline the target place. Nearest tenth: the 4 in 3.462.
Look ONLY at the digit immediately to its right: 6.
5 or more: round the target digit up. 4 or less: keep it. 6 ≥ 5, so 4 becomes 5.
Drop the digits to the right (or make them zeros in a whole number): 3.5.
Check: 3.462 is between 3.4 and 3.5, past the halfway point 3.45, so 3.5 is nearer. ✓ Nearest hundredth: 3.46; nearest whole: 3.

teach.caption: When a 9 rounds up it becomes 10 and carries: 3.96 → 4.0, never 3.10.
The halfway point (3.45) itself rounds up.

teach.text: Rounding slips the TEAS uses: truncating instead of rounding (3.47 → 3.4 to the nearest tenth; it is 3.5), rounding to the wrong place (tens instead of tenths), and botching a 9 (3.96 → 3.10 or 3.9; it is 4.0).

teach.body: In a multi-step problem, keep full values until the final answer, then round once to the place the question asks for. Rounding early carries an error forward. Example: 2.47 × 3 = 7.41, which rounds to 7.4. Round 2.47 to 2.5 first and you get 7.5, a different answer. Only round early when the stem tells you to.

teach.caption: Rounding both numbers UP overestimates; rounding both DOWN underestimates.
Here the normal rule would give 4 buses (too few) and 7 items (can't afford).

teach.h: Worked example: estimating a grocery bill
items: Round each to the nearest dollar: 4 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 + 1 = $19.
Check: the estimate ($19) is within a few cents of the exact total. ✓

teach.h: Scenario: Marisol plans a vaccine clinic
teach.body: Marisol Ortiz, a nursing applicant volunteering at a flu clinic, finds a 10 mL vial gives 10 ÷ 0.75 = 13.33... doses. Only complete doses count, so round DOWN: 13 full doses. She needs syringes for 250 patients in boxes of 24: 250 ÷ 24 = 10.42 boxes. She needs enough, so round UP: 11 boxes. Check: 13 × 0.75 = 9.75 mL ≤ 10 and 11 × 24 = 264 ≥ 250. ✓

items: Look at the one digit right of the target place: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less keeps.
A 9 that rounds up carries into the next place (3.96 → 4.0).
Round once, at the end, to the place the question names.
Context: round up for "enough," down for "complete units."
Estimate with compatible numbers, clustering and benchmarks to check answers.

summary: You can now round to any place, carry correctly through 9s, and decide when a real situation demands rounding up or down. You can also estimate quickly with compatible numbers, clustering and benchmark fractions, and avoid rounding too early.

A.why: The hundredths digit is 8. The next digit is 6 (5 or more), so round up: 47.09.

whyNot.0: 47.08 truncates (cuts off) the digits instead of rounding; the 6 means round up.
whyNot.2: 47.1 rounds to the nearest tenth, the wrong place.
whyNot.3: 47.086 rounds to the nearest thousandth, the wrong place.

A.q: A clinic sees 74 patients, and each needs 3 syringes. Syringes come in boxes of 50. How many boxes must the clinic order?
A.why: Syringes: 74 × 3 = 222. Boxes: 222 ÷ 50 = 4.44. The clinic needs enough, so round up: 5 boxes. Check: 4 boxes hold only 200.

whyNot.0: 2 divides 74 by 50 and forgets that each patient needs 3 syringes.
whyNot.1: 4 rounds 4.44 down, which leaves the clinic 22 syringes short.
whyNot.3: 222 is the number of syringes, an intermediate step, not boxes.

A.q: Which is the best estimate of 6.92 × 49.7?

whyNot.1: 35 has the decimal point one place too far left.
whyNot.2: 300 truncates 6.92 to 6 (front-end) instead of rounding to 7, which loses almost 50.
whyNot.3: 3,500 has the decimal point one place too far right.

B.q: A patient's temperature reads 99.85°F. What is this rounded to the nearest tenth?
B.why: The tenths digit is 8 and the next digit is 5. 5 or more rounds up, so 99.9°F.

whyNot.0: 99.8°F rounds a 5 down; a 5 rounds up.
whyNot.2: 100.0°F rounds to the nearest whole degree, the wrong place.
whyNot.3: 99.0°F cuts off everything after the ones place.

B.q: A 20 mL vial contains medication given in 1.5 mL doses. How many full doses can be drawn from the vial?
B.why: 20 ÷ 1.5 = 13.33... Only complete doses count, so round down: 13. Check: 13 × 1.5 = 19.5 mL ≤ 20.

whyNot.0: 10 rounds the dose to 2 mL before dividing (20 ÷ 2), rounding too early.
whyNot.1: 14 rounds up, but 14 × 1.5 = 21 mL is more than the vial holds.

B.q: Which is the best estimate of 26% of $398?

whyNot.2: $1,000 has the decimal point one place too far right (10 times too big).
whyNot.3: $10 has the decimal point one place too far left.

C.q: A recipe uses 1.375 cups of oats per batch. How many cups are needed for 7 batches? Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
C.why: Keep full values, round at the end: 1.375 × 7 = 9.625. The digit after the tenths is 2, so 9.6.

whyNot.0: 9.8 rounds 1.375 to 1.4 first (1.4 × 7), carrying the rounding error.
whyNot.1: 9.7 rounds 1.375 to 1.38 first (1.38 × 7 = 9.66), then rounds again.
whyNot.3: 9.63 rounds to the nearest hundredth, not the nearest tenth.

C.q: Nadia buys items costing $4.85, $7.62 and $3.71 and wants an estimate that is sure NOT to be less than the real total. Which estimate should she use?
C.why: Rounding every price UP guarantees an overestimate: 5 + 8 + 4 = $17, and the exact total is $16.18.

whyNot.0: Rounding every price down gives an underestimate ($14 < $16.18).
whyNot.1: Rounding 7.62 down to 7 makes this $16, which is below the exact $16.18.
whyNot.2: Cutting off the hundredths lowers every price, so $16.10 is below $16.18.

C.q: A hospital system recorded 1,486,512 patient visits last year. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
C.why: The ten-thousands digit is 8 (1,4[8]6,512). The next digit is 6, so round up to 9 and zero the rest: 1,490,000.

whyNot.0: 1,480,000 truncates; the 6 to the right means round up.
whyNot.2: 1,500,000 rounds to the nearest hundred thousand, the wrong place.
whyNot.3: 1,487,000 rounds to the nearest thousand, the wrong place.

reteach.title: Rounding is choosing the nearer exit
reteach.question: You are driving between highway exits 40 and 50 and you are at mile 47. Which exit is nearer, and how does that picture explain the rounding rule and the up-or-down decisions?

blocks.body: At mile 47 you are 7 miles past exit 40 and 3 miles before exit 50, so exit 50 is nearer: 47 rounds to 50. At mile 45 you are exactly halfway, and the rule says take the exit ahead: 45 rounds up to 50. Context can override "nearest": if you need gas and the station is only at exit 50, you drive on (round up). If your ticket only covers complete zones, you stop at the last one you reached (round down).

items: 3.462 to the nearest tenth: the "exits" are 3.4 and 3.5, halfway is 3.45.
3.462 is past 3.45, so it rounds to 3.5.
Only the digit right after the target place (6) decides; later digits don't matter.

blocks.text: Cutting a number off is not rounding: mile 47 is not "exit 40" just because it starts with a 4.

explain.body: Look only at the digit immediately right of the target place. Never round in stages from the far right: 0.0749 to the nearest hundredth looks at the 4, so it stays 0.07.

test.why: The hundredths digit is 7; the digit after it is 4, so keep the 7: 0.07.

whyNot.0: 0.08 rounds in stages (0.0749 → 0.075 → 0.08); only the digit right after the target counts.

explain.body: Carry full values through every step, then round the final answer once. 3.45 × 2.8 = 9.66, which rounds to 9.7.

test.q: Compute 3.45 × 2.8. Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
test.why: 3.45 × 2.8 = 9.66. The digit after the tenths is 6, so round up: 9.7.

whyNot.2: 9.66 is not rounded to the nearest tenth.

explain.body: If you must have enough (packs, boxes, buses), round up. If only complete units count (full doses, items you can afford), round down, whatever the digit.

steps.label: Need enough?
steps.sub: yes: every pair must be covered

test.q: A charge nurse needs 46 pairs of compression socks. They come in packs of 6 pairs. How many packs must she order?
test.why: 46 ÷ 6 = 7.67. She needs enough, so round up: 8 packs. Check: 7 packs hold only 42 pairs.

whyNot.0: 7 rounds down and leaves her 4 pairs short.
whyNot.3: 46 is the number of pairs needed, not packs.

explain.body: When several values sit near one number, multiply that number by how many values there are. Four values near 10 add to about 4 × 10 = 40.

test.q: Which is the best estimate of 9.87 + 10.21 + 9.94 + 10.05?
test.why: All four values are close to 10, so the sum is about 4 × 10 = 40. (Exact: 40.07.)

whyNot.1: 4 counts the values instead of adding them.
whyNot.2: 400 has the decimal point one place too far right.
